data.reason: The KPI's main goal is town-wide on_time_deliveries, with p95_wait_s, max_wait_s and unfinished as watched goals (K1). Option 2 lowers on-time from 85.0 to 80.6 (-4.4, 0/5 seeds improved), so it fails the main goal on every seed. Late rises from 2.4 to 6.8. p95_wait_s rises from 103 to 173, and the lowest on-time rate falls from 0.94 to 0.92. The only customer-side gain is max_wait_s falling from 351 to 312, a single worst case that does not offset a broad worsening of typical tail waits. Road violations rise from 29.4 to 51.6 and blocked s from 1078 to 1810, so road-rule enforcement would weaken sharply while the cause of the violation rise flagged since D1 is still unexamined. This is the same pattern that led to rejecting the change in D3 (-3.0, 0/5; violations 34.8 -> 58.0). Quiet demand has not removed the harm; the relative customer loss is larger now. I follow the LLM's recommendation. The vote is A no, B no, C yes, so keeping v3 matches the majority. On a season-dependent sanction in general: I do not rule it out in principle. It would be acceptable only if the quiet-period measurement showed no customer cost, and this one does not. It would also add a busy-season revert, a new operational risk that has not been measured. No contract change is involved, so customers' promised times are unaffected. I acknowledge that this is the sixth period without a real mitigation for C (9.6 vs about 26-27). That gap is a serious and growing cost to C's trust and to the operator's credibility, and I take responsibility for it on behalf of the operator. Option 2 would deliver C's gain (9.6 -> 28.6) by moving the cost onto customers and road safety. D4 and D5 committed against that trade. The mitigation must come through negotiated compensation or a rule that targets C's bottleneck, measured on the same seeds. Because rule changes keep failing to deliver it, I am escalating compensation as a concrete next step.
assumptions: Same-seed measurements for next period are representative of option 2's effect in quiet periods.
The rise in road violations under option 2 reflects weaker enforcement rather than a measurement artifact.
Customers value p95 wait and on-time delivery more than a lower single worst wait.
C's low utility can be addressed by compensation or a targeted rule without customer cost.
unknowns: Cause and safety relevance of road violation increases since D1.
What specifically limits C's utility under v3.
Whether C would accept negotiated compensation, and how C will react to a sixth period without mitigation.
Whether an intermediate sanction_lambda (e.g. 0.25) would help C with smaller customer cost.
Per-seed effect of hold_limit 40s on C and on customers.
